claims.text: Post-deposition annealing in a mildly oxidizing atmosphere will induce a coherent, nanocrystalline oxide layer on a high-entropy-alloy surface.
The annealing-induced oxide layer will significantly reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate over a wide service-temperature range.
A relevant initial material can be an as-deposited nanocrystalline refractory HEA film.
The as-deposited HEA lacks a preformed lubricious surface oxide layer.
Controlled annealing in a mildly oxidizing environment can grow a thin, uniform, and adherent lubricious oxide film on the alloy.
The beneficial tribological effect will remain effective from room temperature to at least 300 °C in ambient air.
The oxide phase forms along surface grain boundaries and on the top surface while remaining nanocrystalline and coherent.
Formation of the oxide phase reduces surface roughness.
The oxide phase establishes a self-lubricating sliding interface.
Selective oxidation of Cu or Mn in an HEA produces a lubricious oxide.
The oxide limits metal-to-metal contact and acts as a barrier to wear during sliding.
At elevated temperatures, the oxide remains stable and reduces abrasive and adhesive wear.
Annealed components may have a room-temperature coefficient of friction 30–50% below that of untreated components.
Annealed components may have a wear rate one to two orders of magnitude below that of untreated components.
The predicted reductions in friction and wear will be maintained across the intended temperature range.
Untreated HEAs exhibit higher friction and accelerated wear because of direct contact and less-protective surface characteristics.
The intervention remains beneficial only while the oxide retains coherence, uniformity, and adhesion during cyclic sliding.
Extreme temperature fluctuations or aggressive chemical environments can destabilize the oxide and limit its effectiveness.
The magnitude of friction and wear improvement and the oxide's long-term stability may depend on alloy composition and processing parameters.
